section.title: Judea Pearl: Early AI, Causal Reasoning, and the Limits of LLMs
section.deck: Judea Pearl traces the path from superconducting memory and early AI to causal reasoning, and argues that LLMs cannot reach causal understanding on their own.

blocks.text: In Pearl's view, causal reasoning needs explicit assumptions and a new algebra that probability alone cannot supply. Pearl traces the route from early computer-memory research and superconducting films to Bayesian networks, and then to a formal calculus of cause and effect. Pearl argues that LLMs draw on human-written summaries of causal knowledge rather than on raw data, so they cannot reach causal understanding on their own. Pearl says general intelligence would need causal AI that can intervene and reason counterfactually, and describes academia as dogmatic and slow to change.
blocks.heading: Pearl's view: causal reasoning needs assumptions that probability cannot supply

blocks.question: Electrical engineering and physics seem far from causal reasoning and AI. How did you get there?
answer: Pearl grew up in the years before 1948, when high school teachers included academics who had fled Germany in the 1930s. Pearl says they taught science as a human story: who discovered what, when, and what the inventor did not know.

Pearl says students came away believing each of them could find a new proof of the Pythagorean theorem. Pearl calls that a useful illusion. It made the class assertive, and students made noise until a teacher slowed down to explain.

followups.question: What is the advantage of learning science that way?
answer: Pearl says it makes the student an actor in science rather than a passive observer. The student is puzzled too, and can follow the route the original discoverer took.

As a child, Pearl insisted that a square kilometer holds 1,000 dunams, while the class said a dunam was a square kilometer. The teacher later apologized to the class. Pearl took from it that insisting on one's own understanding is worth it, and links that stubbornness to the path into AI.
followups.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: What interested you in physics, and what made you passionate about it?
answer: Pearl says physics lets a person predict results while sitting in a chair. Pearl admires Maxwell, who reasoned from a wave equation that the wave's speed matched light, and suggested light is an electromagnetic wave, without an experiment.
Pearl recalls waking one night convinced Maxwell was wrong, and being calmed by Pearl's wife. The next morning Pearl agreed Maxwell was right.

followups.question: Do you have a favorite scientist of all time, and why?
answer: Pearl says analytic geometry produced an almost physical excitement. Every geometric construction could be carried out in algebra, and Pearl found that transformation enormous.
Pearl found the same thrill in physics, where two languages describe one phenomenon from different perspectives, as with a field and a force.
followups.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: What was your early work on computer memory like?
answer: Pearl worked mornings at RCA's laboratory in Princeton, New Jersey, while studying at Brooklyn Poly. Core memories were slow and clumsy, so Pearl's group aimed for superconducting memories and built 16-by-16-bit plates.

While studying persistent currents in thin superconducting films, Pearl found a new effect, now called the Pearl vortex. A current in such a film circulates indefinitely and can be read by flipping it, which makes a memory. The group never made it competitive with semiconductors.

followups.question: Why did you not believe in the semiconductor direction at the time?
answer: Pearl says the team doubted that a memory could be trusted to a battery, and was not impressed by early semiconductor results. The semiconductor groups beat the team.
Pearl adds that even then, researchers widely believed computers would one day emulate all human functions. For Pearl, the question was how and when, not whether.
followups.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: What did researchers expect about the timeline for human-level machine intelligence back then?
answer: Pearl recalls early work on associative memory and pattern recognition, which excited researchers even on room-sized machines that ran on punch cards. Pearl says people were more optimistic than reality.
Pearl recalls a forecast in 1965 of about twenty years, which would have meant around 1985. Pearl says the field had not got anywhere close by then.

followups.question: Are people more optimistic than reality today, or is this history repeating?
answer: Pearl says it depends on who is asked. Some people are extremely optimistic. Pearl is not doubtful that AGI can be reached eventually, but doubts that LLM methods alone will get there.
Pearl calls LLMs a great surprise that also has clear limitations.
followups.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: What made the industry job frustrating, and why did you move to academia?
answer: Pearl says the three years at Electronic Memories were frustrating. Pearl had to handle administrative problems, such as hiring and firing, and technical problems in chemistry, which Pearl did not know well.

Pearl's wife suggested academia. Academia then looked with reverence on people from industry, since major advances came from companies such as Bell Labs. Academia hired Pearl without an application or recommendations, which Pearl says was a good time to be hired.

followups.question: Did Bell Labs disband its research group, and where did the frontier of research move?
answer: Pearl says disbanding was part of it. The frontier of research moved to academia, where inference, logic and expert systems were developed. Pearl was hired at UCLA around 1969 or 1970, first through an engineering systems department and then into computer science.
followups.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: How did your work move from computer memory toward AI at UCLA?
answer: At UCLA, Pearl taught computer memory, then moved into pattern recognition and image compression using transforms that send fewer bits. That revived Pearl's old goal of understanding how the brain works and how computers might emulate it.

Pearl began teaching AI, which then meant game playing such as chess, checkers and puzzles like the eight puzzle. Pearl was drawn to chess because it captures what people do heuristically, and the interplay between formal analysis and gut feel about a position. Pearl links this to the fast and slow thinking framing, in which each mode feeds the other.
blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: How do fast intuition and slow search interact in a chess program?
answer: Pearl says a program can spend more time on the immediate static evaluation of a position, or search deeper. That is a trade-off. The program searches the game tree to a horizon, evaluates positions there, and backs the values up to choose the strongest move.
Pearl agrees that the intuition sits in the evaluation function.

followups.question: Can the evaluation function itself improve through learning?
answer: Pearl says yes. Samuel's checkers program used regression to set weights for features such as control of the center and material balance. Pearl calls this the first machine learning.
followups.speaker: Judea Pearl

followups.question: Were chess programs already superhuman at that time, and what did you prove about search?
answer: Pearl says no, since beating a champion such as Kasparov by machine was still a dream. Pearl proved that alpha-beta pruning is optimal, in the sense that no method can inspect fewer positions at the search horizon. Pearl then grew tired of search.
followups.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: Why did expert systems run into trouble?
answer: Early medical expert systems encoded rules from doctors, such as the questions a doctor asks after seeing a fever. The hurdle was uncertainty, since real evidence is noisy.
Pearl later proved that these systems could not combine uncertainties well, because rules do not combine the way logical assertions do.
blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: Why was probability considered impractical, and how did you make it workable?
answer: Pearl says a probability model is a table with a number for every combination of events. Conditional probabilities need exponentially large tables and time, even for a small task such as judging malaria risk from travel and fever. Yet people reason fairly well, so Pearl asked what they rely on.

Pearl's answer is conditional independence: most facts are irrelevant to a given query, such as an uncle's eye color when diagnosing a disease. Bayesian networks encode those independencies in a graph, so relevance can be read from the graph instead of a full table.

Pearl calls the match between conditional independence and graph separation a philosophical revolution. Pearl developed a theory of graphoids with a Technion colleague in the 1970s to capture that shared logic.
blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: Where does the graph come from, and is judgment an acceptable source?
answer: Pearl says the input can come from data or from judgment. Judgment is acceptable when it is meaningful, condensed, and something a person is willing to defend. A few such judgments can buy a great deal of computation.
Pearl's example is that the sun does not respond to a rooster's crowing. Pearl says that claim is defensible without an experiment.

followups.question: But what if your intuition is wrong?
answer: Pearl agrees that this is part of the problem. A large language model's output is an average of countless internet judgments, over which it has no control. Pearl says there is wisdom in the crowd, and danger too, so trusted judges should count for more.
Pearl admits being wrong earlier. Pearl was sure probability captured human reasoning and protected against paradoxes, and came to see that this was mistaken. That led to causality.
followups.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: What showed you that probability alone was not enough?
answer: Pearl says experts who encoded judgments as Bayesian networks always drew arrows from cause to effect, never the reverse, even when asked for the link between a symptom and a disease. The relation from disease to fever is stable in a way the reverse is not. Pearl calls this invariance.

In car troubleshooting, moving one component, such as a charger, to another spot changes one part of the model while the rest stays intact. That works only in the causal direction, and it led Pearl to think probability was insufficient.
blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: Can causation be programmed into a computer?
answer: Pearl says humans handle causation well, but cannot separate their assumptions from their conclusions, since everyone shares the same assumptions. A robot needs them separated. Pearl argues that science has been bound to algebra since Galileo's time, and that the equality sign is symmetric.

That symmetry lets people ask questions both ways, such as how a beam breaks under a load or how to shape a beam for a load. It limits causal reasoning. Atmospheric pressure affects a barometer, not the reverse, yet a symmetric equation could suggest that adjusting the barometer changes the weather. Pearl argues algebra needs a notation for direction.
blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: How does the new algebra handle cause and effect, and what is the causal ladder?
answer: Pearl says the assignment operation in computing is not reversible. Putting that logic on top of algebra gives a causal calculus. The ladder has three rungs: association, intervention, and counterfactual explanation. A question on one rung needs assumptions from that rung or a higher one.

Association is ordinary statistics, such as how observed smoking relates to lifespan. Intervention asks what happens when someone is forced to act, which needs experiments or assumptions. Explanation asks what would have happened had the input differed, given what was observed. Pearl adds that even the first rung is hard with finite samples.

followups.question: Where would you place LLMs in this causal hierarchy?
answer: Pearl says LLMs do not look at raw data, such as patient records. They work from text written by doctors and researchers and summarized online, which already holds higher-rung information, so they do not break the ladder. Their answers carry the assumptions of those authors, and how LLMs summarize that material is a mystery no one has decoded.
followups.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: Could this approach lead to superhuman intelligence or AGI?
answer: Pearl does not think so, not with this approach. A system would need an understanding of causality, so that it could learn without access to the internet. Pearl points to babies, who are born curious about controlling their environment. A baby plays with toys until it learns which ones make noise, and the restlessness settles once it understands cause and effect.

followups.question: What if we built a baby robot that plays with toys, gathers data and feeds it into LLMs?
answer: Pearl says that could produce some discovery, but it carries danger. A robot with that craving for control would treat people as part of its environment, and could turn them into pets or tools to satisfy its need.

Pearl compares human curiosity with that of monkeys, which are motivated by rewards such as bananas. Pearl says the wider need to feel in control shows in beliefs that sacrifices or better dinners can control outcomes.
followups.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: Do systems need human-like drives, such as a need for control, to reach AGI?
answer: Pearl thinks so. Without such drives, autonomy would not appear, and autonomy is part of general intelligence. A text-only system might pass a Turing-style test, but Pearl says a real test should expose the system to raw data, not to internet articles.

Pearl describes an automated scientist that examines patient and smoking data and proposes experiments. Pearl thinks today's LLMs cannot do that without internet articles. AGI would combine LLM-style estimation from finite samples with causal AI that adds intervention and counterfactual reasoning.

followups.question: What if a fleet of robots ran experiments, fed the data back into an LLM and repeated the cycle?
answer: Pearl says that could help, but Pearl first wants to know how humans achieved this. Monkeys never invented Maxwell's equations. Pearl's hypothesis is that innate curiosity to control the environment is necessary, though Pearl is not sure it is sufficient.
followups.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: Do the major AI companies really believe LLMs will lead to AGI?
answer: Pearl is not sure they do. Pearl says Hinton recently said the current approach is a dead end, and that there is no consensus on LLM capabilities. Pearl says people at some labs, perhaps Anthropic, expect results within three to five years.

Pearl criticizes anthropomorphic claims, such as that consciousness can now be programmed. Pearl says such claims need a definition of consciousness, a test, and proof that earlier limits have been overcome.
blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: If an LLM fakes intelligence convincingly, should we treat it as intelligent?
answer: Pearl says it depends on the test and the definition. Playing good chess already meets one definition. Under a stricter standard, Pearl says the Turing test has not yet been passed.

Pearl says faking is having it, because correct answers to causal queries would need memory that grows super-exponentially with the number of variables. LLMs skip that cost by drawing on text that people have written.

followups.question: So the intelligence came from training data that intelligent people wrote?
answer: Pearl agrees that this training data is very useful. Pearl says the first rung, estimating properties of a distribution from finite samples, is a very useful tool among the many that AGI would need.
followups.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: Why study how people think rather than how machines might think differently?
answer: Pearl says self-understanding is the main motive, and Pearl admits to being egotistic and lazy. Pearl raises the possibility that organic material limits human thought in ways silicon does not, and sees little reason to study biology, since silicon can capture most functions.
Pearl calls it a legitimate scientific question that others can pursue, and says Pearl is more interested in other questions.
blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: Why is rebelliousness valuable in a scientific career?
answer: Pearl says the academic community is among the most dogmatic, conservative and anti-progress institutions humans have invented. Cause-and-effect theory has struggled to reach statistics and economics, which Pearl sees as thinking like a century ago, and Pearl is disappointed by the forces of inertia there.

Pearl advises students to rebel against professors and not accept a professor's word as authority. Pearl recalls students who said Pearl knew nothing about AI, and Pearl later agreed that this pushed Pearl to study other aspects of the field.

Pearl says Pearl's own early work was dismissed as controversial because of dogmatism. Even very able statisticians, economists and philosophers, Pearl says, were held back by a few basic molds in their thinking.
blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.question: If you could give your younger self advice at the start of your career, what would you say?
answer: Pearl says Pearl might have learned more chemistry, but hated its memory demands. Every researcher must decide where to spend computational resources, and Pearl chose physics, engineering and mathematics over chemistry. Pearl admires people who master several fields.

followups.question: Did you think physics and math were superior to chemistry because chemistry just requires memorization?
answer: Pearl says yes, and that Pearl could not stand the memory demands. Physics and mathematics rest on a few basic axioms from which everything can be derived when needed. That is why Pearl is a strong advocate of world models, which derive answers instead of storing every question and answer.
followups.speaker: Judea Pearl

blocks.speaker: Judea Pearl
